passages.t: Chosen, and the lion has roared
passages.happening:
‘Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, O children of Israel’ (verse 1), the whole family he brought up out of Egypt. ‘Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities’ (verse 2).

Then Amos asks a string of questions. Can two walk together without agreeing where to go (verse 3)? Does a lion roar when it has no prey (verse 4)? Does a bird land in a snare with no bait (verse 5)? ‘If a ram’s horn sounds in a city, do the people not tremble? If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?’ (verse 6). The Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his plan to his servants the prophets (verse 7). ‘The lion has roared’, who will not fear? ‘The Lord GOD has spoken’, who will not prophesy (verse 8)?
passages.hearers:
Verse 2 is a startling turn. Israel expected its election to mean protection. God says it means accountability. To be known by God, chosen out of all the families of the earth, is to be held to a higher standard, not excused from one.

Verses 3 to 8 are questions drawn from everyday life: two people walking together, a lion's roar, a bird in a trap, a trumpet in a city. Each points to a cause behind an effect. The chain climbs to the claim that disaster in a city comes from the LORD, and then to its real point. When God speaks, the prophet cannot keep quiet. Amos is explaining why a herdsman from Judah is standing in Bethel saying hard things. He has no choice.

The lion picks up the roar of 1:2, and it will return in verse 12.
passages.later: God's promise to Abraham reached ‘all the families of the earth’ (Genesis 12:3), and the law told Israel it was chosen not because it was great but because the LORD loved it (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). Jeremiah too said the word was like a fire he could not hold in (Jeremiah 20:9).
passages.hard:
Does verse 6 mean that God causes every disaster?

The Hebrew word for calamity is the common word for evil or harm, which is why some older translations read it as evil. The setting is judgment on a rebellious nation, and Amos's point is that Israel should not read its coming disaster as chance or as the work of other gods. It is the LORD's doing, and it carries a message. Many theologians see here God's rule over history, suffering included, without making God the author of moral evil; human agents like Assyria remain responsible for their cruelty. Others stress that the verse belongs to Israel's covenant setting and must not be turned into a rule that every disaster is a punishment, which Scripture elsewhere resists, in Job and in Jesus' own words. What the verse does teach is that God is not absent from catastrophe, and that his people should listen for what he is saying through it.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: Israel thought being chosen made it safe. Ask whether you have treated God's grace to you as a reason to take sin lightly. And ask what God has said to you that you have been keeping quiet about.

passages.happening:
Proclaim it to the strongholds of Ashdod and of Egypt: let them gather on the mountains of Samaria and see the unrest and oppression in the city (verse 9). The people of Samaria do not know how to do right, and they store up violence in their fortresses (verse 10). So an enemy will surround the land and plunder them (verse 11).

‘As the shepherd snatches from the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear’, so the Israelites of Samaria will be rescued with only the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch (verse 12). On the day God punishes Israel he will destroy the altars of Bethel, and the horns of the altar will be cut off (verse 14). ‘I will tear down the winter house along with the summer house; the houses of ivory will also perish’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The chapter becomes a trial. Foreign nations, Philistines and Egyptians, are called as witnesses to what goes on in Samaria. Even they will be shocked.

Samaria had been the northern capital since King Omri built it on a high, easily defended hill in the early ninth century BC. Under Jeroboam II it was the center of the kingdom's wealth. The Bible mentions an ivory house built by Ahab, and excavations at Samaria found many fragments of carved ivory for furniture and walls, generally dated to the ninth and eighth centuries BC. Wealthy families sometimes kept separate houses for the cool rainy season and the hot summer. Amos names both and says both will fall.

Verse 12 draws on shepherding law. A shepherd who lost an animal to a wild beast could clear himself by bringing the owner what was left, as proof that it was killed and not stolen. What is rescued of Samaria will only prove that the city is gone. The horns of an altar were the projections at its corners, where a person fleeing for his life could hold on to claim sanctuary. To cut them off is to say there will be no refuge at Bethel. Within about forty years Assyria took Samaria, and King Josiah of Judah later tore down the altar at Bethel.
passages.later: The law let a shepherd bring the remains of a torn animal as evidence (Exodus 22:13). Ahab's ivory house is named in 1 Kings 22:39, and Josiah tore down the altar at Bethel (2 Kings 23:15).
passages.asks: Even the Philistines and Egyptians are called to look at Samaria's oppression. Ask what an outsider would see if they looked closely at how your community treats the weak. And ask what you are storing up in your own strongholds.
